D.t: Charles Booker trails by 11.1 and wins 5% of simulations. Closing it takes about 92,267 voters switching sides, or 184,534 more net votes from new turnout.
In 8 of 10 simulations the result lands between R +19.6 and R +2.3. Only an unusual polling error changes the winner.

The biggest vote banks for Democrats: Jefferson, a projected net 114,613 votes; Fayette, a projected net 43,969 votes; Franklin, a projected net 4,018 votes. Every point of extra turnout here is worth more than persuasion anywhere else.
The large counties within 12 points: Kenton, R +4.4, 3.7% of the vote; Warren, R +9.1, 2.7% of the vote; Campbell, R +1.8, 2.2% of the vote; Madison, R +11.9, 2.2% of the vote.

D.h: Where you run behind the 2024 map
D.t: Against the 2024 presidential vote, Charles Booker runs furthest behind in Laurel, Pulaski, Boone. That is where the forecast sees voters who backed your side two years ago and have not come back yet.

Groups big enough to move the race: White voters, 90% of voters, 41 to 59, where a 5 point gain is worth 4.53 points; Voters who cast ballots in 2022 and 2024, 69% of voters, 44 to 56, where a 5 point gain is worth 3.44 points; Voters without a degree, 67% of voters, 41 to 59, where a 5 point gain is worth 3.36 points.
The forecast's worst groups for Charles Booker: Immigration voters 15 to 85, Small counties 32 to 68, Other issue voters 40 to 60. Cutting the loss here is often cheaper than winning new groups.
$310K cash against $2.3M. Outspent: lean on earned media, digital, field and the outside groups, and pick the two or three media markets that decide it.
Registered Democrats cast 53% of the 192,709 ballots in Kentucky so far, against 47% for the other party. That is 5.7 points better for Democrats than the forecast expected by now.

D.h: What the ballots so far say
D.t: The early vote has moved this forecast 1.1 points toward Charles Booker. Bank it: chase the remaining mail ballots and low propensity voters who have not voted.
